editorial.note: Scientists spotted what appear to be thunderheads on Jupiter bright white cumulus clouds similar to those that bring thunderstorms on Earth, at the outer edges of Jupiter Great Red Spot.
First evidence of a ring around the planet Jupiter is seen in this photograph taken by NASA's Voyager 1 on March 4, 1979.
This view of the north polar region of the Moon was obtained by NASA Galileo camera during the spacecraft flyby of the Earth-Moon system on December 7 and 8, 1992.
This false-color mosaic of part of the Moon was constructed from 54 images taken by the imaging system aboard NASA Galileo as the spacecraft flew past the Moon on December 7, 1992.

This false-color photograph is a composite of 15 images of the Moon taken through three color filters NASA Galileo solid-state imaging system during the spacecraft passage through the Earth-Moon system on December 8, 1992.
This image of the crescent moon was obtained by the Galileo Solid State imaging system on December 8 at 5 a.m. PST as NASA Galileo spacecraft neared the Earth.

This image of the western hemisphere of the Moon was taken through a green filter by NASA Galileo spacecraft at 9:35 a.m. PST Dec. 9 at a range of about 350,000 miles. In the center is the Orientale Basin.
These color visualizations of the Moon were obtained by NASA Galileo spacecraft as it left the Earth after completing its first Earth Gravity Assist. The images were acquired Dec. 8-9, 1990.

This image of the moon was obtained by the Galileo Solid State imaging system on Dec. 8 at 7 p.m. PST as NASA Galileo spacecraft passed the Earth and was able to view the lunar surface from a vantage point not possible from the Earth.
This color image of the Moon was taken by NASA Galileo spacecraft at 9:35 a.m. PST Dec. 9, 1990, at a range of about 350,000 miles.

These pictures of the Moon were taken by NASA Galileo spacecraft at right photo Dec.8, 1990 from a distance of almost 220,000 miles, and at left photo Dec. 9, 1990 at a range of more than 350,000 miles.

117008.title: Saturn With Rhea and Dione True Color
117008.creator: NASA/JPL

editorial.note: NASA Voyager 2 took this true color photograph of Saturn on July 21, 1981. The moons Rhea and Dione appear as blue dots to the south and southeast of Saturn, respectively.
Saturn and two of its moons, Tethys above and Dione, were photographed by Voyager 1 on November 3, 1980, from 13 million kilometers 8 million miles.

117010.title: Saturn - Brown Ovals in Northern Hemisphere
117010.creator: NASA/JPL

editorial.note: Two brown ovals, at right, some 10,000 km 6,000 miles across, were found at approximately 40` and 60` latitude in Saturn northern hemisphere by NASA Voyager 1. The photo was taken on November 7, 1980.

117011.title: Saturn - False Color of Southern Hemisphere
117011.creator: NASA/JPL

editorial.note: This false-color image of Saturn southern hemisphere taken by NASA Voyager 1 on Nov. 6, 1980, shows the unique red oval cloud feature located at 55 degrees south latitude.
Saturn storms observed by NASA Voyager, Aug. 5, 2004. Voyager 1 and 2 observed radio signals from lightning which were interpreted as being from a persistent, low-latitude storm system.

117013.title: Saturn -- Ribbon-like Wave Structure in Atmosphere
117013.creator: NASA/JPL

editorial.note: A view of Saturn clouds extending from 40` to 60` N latitude shows a ribbon-like wave structure in the south with small convective features marking a westward jet in the north. This image was obtained on November 10, 1980 by NASA Voyager 1.

This false color picture of Saturn’s northern hemisphere was assembled from ultraviolet, violet and green images obtained Aug. 19, 1998 by NASA's Voyager 2. The several weather patterns evident include three spots flowing westward.

117015.title: Jupiter with Satellites Io and Europa
117015.creator: NASA/JPL

editorial.note: NASA Voyager 1 took this photo of Jupiter and two of its satellites Io, left, and Europa on Feb. 13, 1979. Io is above Jupiter Great Red Spot; Europa is above Jupiter clouds. The poles are dark and reddish.

Jupiter satellite Io poses before the giant planet in this photo returned January 17, 1979. The satellite shadow can be seen falling on the face of Jupiter at left. Io is traveling from left to right in its orbit around Jupiter.
This computer generated map of Jupiter was made from 10 color images of Jupiter taken Feb. 1, 1979, by NASA Voyager 1, during a single, 10 hour rotation of the planet.

This processed color image of Jupiter was produced in 1990 by the U.S. Geological Survey from a Voyager image captured in 1979. Zones of light-colored, ascending clouds alternate with bands of dark, descending clouds.

These mosaics of Jupiter's night side show the Jovian aurora at approximately 45 minute intervals as the auroral ring rotated with the planet below the spacecraft. The images were obtained by NASA's Galileo spacecraft.
Jupiter, its Great Red Spot and three of its four largest satellites are visible in this photo taken Feb. 5, 1979, by Voyager 1. Io, Europa, and Callisto are seen against Jupiter disk.

This view of Jupiter Great Red Spot is a mosaic of two images taken by NASA Galileo spacecraft. The Great Red Spot is a storm in Jupiter atmosphere and is at least 300 years-old. The image was taken on June 26, 1996.

117023.title: Jupiter - Io In Front of Jupiter Turbulent Clouds
117023.creator: NASA/JPL

editorial.note: This photograph of the southern hemisphere of Jupiter was obtained by NASA's Voyager 2 on June 25, 1979. Seen in front of the turbulent clouds of the planet is Io, the innermost of the large Galilean satellites of Jupiter.

117024.title: Jupiter Great Red Spot and White Ovals
117024.creator: NASA/JPL

editorial.note: This photo of Jupiter was taken by NASA Voyager 1 on March 1, 1979. The photo shows Jupiter Great Red Spot upper right and the turbulent region immediately to the west.

This is one of the highest resolution images ever recorded of Jupiter temperature field. It was obtained by NASA Galileo mission. This map, shown in the lower panel, indicates the forces powering Jovian winds.
NASA Voyager 1 took this picture of the planet Jupiter on Jan. 6, 1979, the first in its three-month-long, close-up investigation of the largest planet.

This image, taken by NASA Galileo spacecraft, shows the darkside of Jupiter, the part not illuminated by sunlight. The curved line crossing from the lower left to the upper right is the auroral arc on the horizon.

This photographic mosaic of images covering an area of 34,000 kilometers by 22,000 kilometers about 21,100 by 13,600 miles in Jupiter equatorial region was taken by NASA Galileo orbiter on December 17, 1996.

NASA Voyager 1 took this photo of Jupiter Feb. 1, 1979. Voyager scientists saw that different colors in clouds around the Great Red Spot imply that the clouds swirl around the spot at varying altitudes.

117031.title: Features of Jupiter Great Red Spot
117031.creator: NASA/JPL-Caltech

editorial.note: This montage features activity in the turbulent region of Jupiter Great Red Spot GRS. Four sets of images of the GRS were taken by NASA Galileo imaging system over an 11.5 hour period on 26 June, 1996.
This mosaic of Jupiter Great Red Spot taken by NASA Voyager 1, shows the area around the northern boundary where a white cloud is seen which extends to east of the region.

This dramatic view of Jupiter Great Red Spot and its surroundings was obtained by NASA Voyager 1 on Feb. 25, 1979. The colorful, wavy cloud pattern to the left of the Red Spot is a region of extraordinarily complex end variable wave motion.

This image returned NASA Voyager 2 shows one of the long dark clouds observed in the North Equatorial Belt of Jupiter. A high, white cloud is seen moving over the darker cloud, providing an indication of the structure of the cloud layers.

117036.title: Mosaic of Jupiter Great Red Spot in the near infrared
117036.creator: NASA/JPL

editorial.note: The mosaic of the Great Red Spot on Jupiter from NASA Galileo orbiter was taken over an 80 second interval beginning at universal time 14 hours, 30 minutes, 23 seconds, on June 26, 1996.

117037.title: Mosaic of Jupiter Great Red Spot in the near infrared
117037.creator: NASA/JPL

editorial.note: This mosaic of the Great Red Spot on Jupiter from NASA Galileo orbiter was taken over an 80 second interval beginning at universal time 14 hours, 30 minutes, 23 seconds, on June 26, 1996.

117038.title: Mosaic of Jupiter Great Red Spot Violet Filter
117038.creator: NASA/JPL-Caltech

editorial.note: This mosaic of the Great Red Spot on Jupiter from NASA Galileo orbiter was taken over a 75 second interval beginning at universal time 4 hours, 18 minutes, 8 seconds on June 26, 1996.

117040.title: True Color Mosaic of Jupiter Belt-Zone Boundary
117040.creator: NASA/JPL-Caltech

editorial.note: Pseudo-true color mosaic of a belt-zone boundary near Jupiter equator. The images that make up the four quadrants of this mosaic were taken within a few minutes of each other by NASA Galileo orbiter.

117041.title: Mosaic of Jupiter Great Red Spot Methane Filter
117041.creator: NASA/JPL

editorial.note: The mosaic of the Great Red Spot on Jupiter from NASA Galileo orbiter was taken over a 76 second interval beginning at universal time 14 hours, 33 minutes, 22 seconds, on June 26, 1996.

117044.title: Hubble Captures Detailed Image of Uranus Atmosphere
117044.creator: NASA/JPL/STScI

editorial.note: NASA Hubble Space Telescope peered deep into Uranus atmosphere to see clear and hazy layers created by a mixture of gases. Using infrared filters, Hubble captured detailed features of three layers of Uranus atmosphere.

117045.title: Venus Cloud Tops Viewed by Hubble
117045.creator: NASA/JPL

editorial.note: Venus Cloud Tops Viewed by Hubble. This is a NASA Hubble Space Telescope ultraviolet-light image of the planet Venus, taken on January 24 1995, when Venus was at a distance of 70.6 million miles 113.6 million kilometers from Earth.
This NASA Hubble Space Telescope image of the planet Uranus reveals the planet rings and bright clouds and a high altitude haze above the planet south pole.

These three NASA Hubble Space Telescope images of the planet Uranus reveal the motion of a pair of bright clouds in the planet southern hemisphere, and a high altitude haze that forms a cap above the planet south pole.
Taking its first peek at Uranus, NASA Hubble Space Telescope Near Infrared Camera and Multi-Object Spectrometer NICMOS detected six distinct clouds in images taken July 28,1997.
These NASA Hubble Space Telescope views of the blue-green planet Neptune provide three snapshots of changing weather conditions.

117056.title: Hubble Finds New Dark Spot on Neptune
117056.creator: NASA/JPL/STScI

editorial.note: In 1995, NASA Hubble Space Telescope discovered a new great dark spot, located in the northern hemisphere of the planet Neptune.

Jupiter aurora on the night side of the planet is seen here at five different wavelengths. Jupiter bright crescent, which is about half illuminated, is out of view to the right in this image taken on April 2, 1997 by NASA Galileo orbiter.

This is a false-color composite of Jupiter northern aurora on the night side of the planet. The height and thickness of the auroral arc, and the small-scale structure were revealed for the first time by NASA Galileo orbiter on April 2, 1997…

117088.title: Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 Fragment W Impact With Jupiter
117088.creator: NASA/JPL

editorial.note: These four images of Jupiter and the luminous night-side impact of fragment W of Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 were taken NASA Galileo spacecraft on July 22, 1994.

The cameras of Voyager 1 on Feb. 14, 1990, pointed back toward the sun and took a series of pictures of the sun and the planets, making the first ever portrait of our solar system as seen from the outside.

117186.title: Heavily Cratered Terrain and Smooth Plain
117186.creator: NASA/JPL

editorial.note: This photograph of Mercury was taken by NASA Mariner 10 spacecraft shows smooth plains areas on Mercury that are thought to be volcanic in origin with lava flows filling in heavily cratered areas.
NASA Mariner 10 spacecraft was coaxed into a third and final encounter with Mercury in March of 1975. This is one of the highest resolution images of Mercury acquired by the spacecraft.
After passing Mercury the first time and making a trip around the Sun, NASA Mariner 10 again flew by Mercury on Sept. 21, 1974.

After passing Mercury the first time and making a trip around the Sun, NASA Mariner 10 again flew by Mercury on Sept. 21, 1974. This encounter brought the spacecraft in front of Mercury in the southern hemisphere.
NASA Mariner 10 took this picture of the densely cratered surface of Mercury when the spacecraft was 18,200 kilometers 8085 miles from the planet on March 29, 1974.

After passing Mercury the first time and making a trip around the Sun, NASA Mariner 10 again flew by Mercury on Sept. 21, 1974. This encounter brought the spacecraft in front of Mercury in the southern hemisphere.

As NASA Mariner 10 approached Mercury at nearly seven miles per second on March 29, 1974, its TV camera took this picture from an altitude of 35,000 kilometers 21,700 miles The picture shows a heavily-cratered surface with many low hills

A dark, smooth, relatively uncratered area on Mercury was photographed two hours after NASA Mariner 10 flew by the planet. The prominent, sharp crater with a central peak is 30 kilometers 19 miles across.
NASA Mariner 10 spacecraft was coaxed into a third and final encounter with Mercury in March of 1975. This is one of the highest resolution images of Mercury acquired by the spacecraft.

117206.title: Fresh Crater in Center of Older Crater Basin
117206.creator: NASA/JPL

editorial.note: A fresh new crater in the center of an older crater basin is shown in this picture of the surface of Mercury taken March 29, 1974 by NASA Mariner 10.
Cratered terrain very similar to that on the Moon is shown in this TV photo of Mercury taken by NASA Mariner 10. Numerous small craters and linear grooves radial to the crater can be seen.

NASA Mariner 10 took this picture some 2 1/2 hours before it passed Mercury on March 29, 1974. The bright-floored crater is the center of a very large bright area which could be seen in pictures from more than two million miles distant

117211.title: Solar System Portrait - Views of 6 Planets
117211.creator: NASA/JPL

editorial.note: These six narrow-angle color images were made from the first ever portrait of the solar system taken by NASA’s Voyager 1, which was more than 4 billion miles from Earth and about 32 degrees above the ecliptic.

This is the first full picture showing both asteroid 243 Ida and its newly discovered moon to be transmitted to Earth from NASA's Galileo spacecraft -- the first conclusive evidence that natural satellites of asteroids exist.
This montage illustrates the various configurations and missions of the three classes of the Saturn vehicles developed by the Marshall Space Flight Center.

This image illustrates the basic differences between the three Saturn launch vehicles developed by the Marshall Space Flight Center. The Saturn I, consisted of two stages, the S-I (eight H-1 engines) and the S-IV (six RL-10 engines).

This is a good cutaway diagram of the Saturn V launch vehicle showing the three stages, the instrument unit, and the Apollo spacecraft. The chart on the right presents the basic technical data in clear metric detail.

A technician checks the systems of the Saturn V instrument unit in a test facility in Huntsville. This instrument unit was flown aboard Apollo 4 on November 7, 1967, which was the first test flight of the Saturn V.
This vintage photograph shows the 138-foot long first stage of the Saturn V being lowered to the ground following a successful static test firing at Marshall Space flight Center's S-1C test stand.
A technician can be seen working atop the white room across from the escape tower of the Apollo 11 spacecraft a few days prior to the launch of the Saturn V moon rocket.

The business end of a Second Stage (S-II) slowly emerges from the shipping container as workers prepare to transport the Saturn V component to the testing facility at MSFC. The Second Stage (S-II) underwent vibration and engine firing tests…

The powerful J-2 engine is prominent in this photograph of a Saturn V Third Stage (S-IVB) resting on a transporter in the Manufacturing Facility at Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama.
The hydrogen-powered second stage is being lowered into place during the final phase of fabrication of the Saturn V moon rocket at North American's Seal Beach, California facility.

Two technicians apply insulation to the outer surface of the S-II second stage booster for the Saturn V moon rocket. The towering 363-foot Saturn V was a multi-stage, multi-engine launch vehicle standing taller than the Statue of Liberty.
This photo shows the Saturn V first stage being lowered to the ground following a successful test to determine the effects of continual vibrations simulating the effects of an actual launch.

This small group of unidentified officials is dwarfed by the gigantic size of the Saturn V first stage (S-1C) at the shipping area of the Manufacturing Engineering Laboratory at Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama.
This Saturn V S-II (second) stage is being lifted into position for a test at the Vehicle Assembly Building at the Kennedy Space Center.
This drawing clearly shows the comparative sizes of the rocket engines used to launch the Saturn vehicles. The RL-10 and the H-1 engines were used to launch the Saturn I rockets.
J-2 engines for the Saturn IB/Saturn V launch vehicles are lined up in the assembly area at Rocketdyne's manufacturing plant in Canoga Park, California.
This photograph shows a Saturn V first stage (S-1C). This stage was assembled at the Manufacturing Engineering Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center.

118442.title: NASA Spacecraft Sees 'Pac-Man' on Saturn Moon
118442.creator: NASA GSFC

editorial.note: NASA release date March 29, 2010 The highest-resolution-yet temperature map and images of Saturn’s icy moon Mimas obtained by NASA’s Cassini spacecraft reveal surprising patterns on the surface of the small moon, including unexpected hot re…

125466.creator: Mir Emad Hassani

editorial.note: Calligraphy from the St. Petersburg album. Calligraphy in nastaliq attributed to Imad al-Hasani, early 17th century. Borders attributed to Muhammad Hadi, mid-18th century. Freer Gallery of Art F1942.17b

133159.creator: Jacques de Gheyn II

147547.creator: Pierre Brebiette
